Yeah, you don't know anyone exactly. You have no idea what he's doing here. Turns out it's actually the person who cleans the office. He shows up more regularly than the rest of the people.

And there's tons and tons of activity. Tons and tons and tons of activity. And expenses grow to seven hundred fifty thousand dollars, and Joe starts noticing a strange phenomenon — there's tons of activity, but not that many results. That's another tough problem that happens in many companies. Everyone's working incredibly hard, there are lots of serious meetings, they produce meeting summaries. But nothing actually happens. Small problem. By the way, the Israeli government — exact same thing. And almost every large organization.

And then Joe starts arguing with Julie because they're not meeting projections. They said they'd have such-and-such number of people and such-and-such revenue, and they're not keeping pace. And they also can't find anyone who'll pay them money. Meaning, they have Providers who are willing to do the work, but since the Providers want to get paid — they probably won't succeed.

And then the pressure grows and Julie decides it's time to start running a very, very strong marketing campaign. And they start the campaign. It costs a lot of money, but the results don't come.

And then arguments between founders. What happens is the fights spill out of the closed room and the board starts getting involved. And the board politely asks Julie to leave. And when the board asks politely and the money is running out — then you also comply. So that's it, Julie is no longer there.

And then they need to fill her position. They take Linda — she's the director of marketing — and she starts handling the marketing activities. And they start cutting expenses by firing fifteen people. They bring expenses down from seven hundred fifty thousand to six hundred thousand, but there's only five million dollars left in the bank.

And then what happens in companies once layoffs start and pressure builds — morale drops. Someone once asked me — tell me, how do you make sure morale in the company stays high? So I said — I don't make sure morale in the company stays high. I make sure the company succeeds. When the company succeeds, morale is high. When the company fails, morale is low. No matter how many massages you give them or what outing you do — it's not relevant. When the company is in a bad state, the mood is bad.

When the company succeeds, everyone's on a high. Company fails — they're on a low.

And then what happens? Almost always the people who leave are the ones you don't want to leave. The ones who stay are the ones you'd fire. What's the logic? Very simple. The ones you don't want to leave — they're actually good and they'll find a job in a minute. The ones who don't leave are the ones who are afraid they won't find a job, so they stay.

So that's why it's very important, if you're getting into trouble and you see you're getting into trouble — make sure to fire the people you don't want to keep, and take all the people you want to keep and promise them that you've got their back and that you won't fire them. You need to do that.

And they're now ready to do another fundraise, but they don't really have much to show. They don't have a business model that works. The market is cooling down. And it's becoming hard to raise money.

Listen. Guys, I'm doing this in a funny way with humor and smiling and so on, but what I'm describing to you here is reality. These aren't jokes. This is how it happens. Nine out of ten companies fail not because they're stupid. This is how it happens. There's a dynamic of very many things and you need to play it more or less like a virtuoso — and you don't have control over very many of the parameters.

And once that virtuosity doesn't work — you fall off the rope. Companies fail over stupid things. They run out of money. The moment they run out of money, they die. And they run out of money many times because the timing wasn't right, didn't work in their favor.

And then people ask me — why do companies fail? I say — because they run out of money. They think I'm giving a stupid answer. So I decided I'd dedicate an entire lecture to showing you how money runs out and how complicated it is. It's not trivial at all.

You need to be a virtuoso to raise money. It's not simple.

They found a new investor. His name is Ray of Hope. Ray of Hope is willing to put in ten million dollars. But he has a few requests. First of all, he's willing to put it in on the condition that the Pre Money of the company is ten million dollars, which means a Down Round. Because before we were at thirty Post, right? So now we've dropped from thirty Post and they're saying — I erased twenty out of the thirty and I'm willing to put ten million dollars in there.

And then smart people asked me — so why did they agree? Exactly. When the existing investors have an option — take it, and the company continues to live — or shut down the company. So most of them said — let's give it another chance. So they're on board.

They invest it in a type of shares called Participating Preferred, and they have First Liquidation Rights.

And one more thing — a small catch. We want a CEO who knows what he's doing. So Joe, please step aside. You already kicked out Julie, but sit on the side. We're not firing you, but let us work in peace. We're bringing in a Turn Around expert. And now I have six people on the board already. Meaning, you can't reach agreement on what day of the week it is. And we added John Stargazes.

First of all, I take my money out before everyone else. That's called Liquidation Preference. I'm first in line. And if there are five — one after another? Ah, that's where the fighting starts. It's not about who's first, it's about who's strongest.

Remember — this is a pure market where everyone fights everyone. And if you think they don't fight — you're wrong. You need to remember — investors are not company builders. They put money in to get money back, preferably more than they invested. That's all they care about. Everything else is this annoying process of building a company. So the terms under which they get their money back — that's the most important thing to them. And that's why there are endless wars around it.

And when there are layers of investors, layer after layer after layer — everyone fights with everyone. Who gets the better protections? Who gets the better return terms? Who wins? Someone who's stronger — in the sense that the company desperately needs them. Everyone is flexible when the company is great and growing and doesn't actually need the money. Then they tell the investor — either you accept my terms or don't come. And then he gets the terms he wants.

Why do I always say be profitable? And then you can sit in the chair and say — I have all the time in the world. You, you need to invest money. I don't. Right, you have seven years to show a return on investment. I've proven that I'm a successful guy. You want to give me money? Give. You don't want to? Go. Next in line is standing in line. That's it.

Liquidation. Board Seat — usually. Now why do they want a Board Seat? Because it gives them access to see how the company behaves and supposedly gives them control power. In practice, it's not really control power, because the board in general — the only real power the board has is to fire the CEO.

Almost always the appointment of the CEO is by the board, so the board can come and say — Jonathan, it was very, very nice. You're a great guy, but starting tomorrow we'll manage without you. That's how it works.

Now what protects the CEO? If the board thinks this CEO has delivered amazing results and without him the company will fail — they don't fire him. If they think this CEO is a danger to the public and certainly a danger to the company — they fire him.

That's the only and primary authority the board has. The board doesn't manage companies. The board doesn't sit and start saying — this deal is good, this deal is not good. The moment the board starts doing that — the company is already in trouble. But they do decide who the CEO will be.

And look at Elon Musk, for example. Right, he does whatever's in his head and the board snaps to attention. Why? Because he's Elon Musk. That's it. He's delivered high financial returns to investors and therefore gets to do whatever he wants.

So you see here again — it's power games, it's money games. There's no right or wrong here, fair or unfair.

Now you need to remember — the investors over time. After four, five, six years there are already several rounds. Five, six people are sitting around the table. Among these five or six people there's almost always a history. Why? Because they're all professional investors. They usually sit in the same geographic area, and they've already been in three previous deals together.

It happened to me, at least in the early stages when I invested and was in charge, that sometimes I sat in board meetings and they were talking and I didn't understand what they were talking about. Why? Because they were settling scores from two companies ago. I had no idea what they were talking about, because they had a history that preceded me by about twenty years. And this happens in every board meeting. People who know each other, they have a lot of scores to settle. It becomes a very, very interesting place, and they also can't agree on almost anything almost ever.

Veto Rights — almost always with Preferred Shares they have Veto Rights that are mainly designed to protect them from all kinds of manipulations.

Look at the list — Change to the Articles of Organization. What are Articles of Organization? That's exactly the document that describes what the rights and obligations are of each type of share. It describes how the board is elected, it describes how decisions are made. It's essentially the constitution of the company.

So obviously if you're going to change the company's constitution — you've changed the company. That's why they say — you can't change anything in this constitution without my consent, because I came in here assuming this is the constitution. And without my consent you can't change the constitution. So this will almost always appear as a veto right of the investor for all Preferred Shares.

For example, Fundraising — we're going to raise more money. Do we even need to raise money? Ready to raise money again? Since the investor is going to be diluted, he wants to have the right to say — no, we're not raising money. Taking a loan — exactly the same thing as an investment, because loans burden the company. He wants veto rights on that. Of course selling the company — usually even if you're making an acquisition you need board approval. Stock offerings, CEO Hiring — and there's more on the list. Usually these are the things that are critical to the company's value and the direction the company is heading. There are veto rights on them almost always.

Anti Dilution — what is Anti Dilution? I hold ten percent of the company today. I want to continue holding ten percent of the company. So usually what it means — Anti Dilution — if the company now raises money in a Down Round, I get some kind of compensation. I want you to increase my number of shares — usually at the expense of the founder or founders. That's usually how it works. It's less common today, but you'll still find Anti Dilution in many, many places.

Pre Emptive Rights — what's that? That's the continuation. I want that if there are more deals and I hold ten percent, you'll allow me to purchase enough shares in the next round to keep me at ten percent. I don't want to slide down. That's called Pre Emptive Rights.

Right of First Refusal — what is Right of First Refusal? It is what it sounds like. If the share price is seven and a half dollars, if I'm willing to pay the same price — I come before you because I'm a stakeholder. I'm already a member of this club, so I have the first right to buy at the price the other party is willing to pay. Not a better price — the exact same price. Give me the right to remain a stakeholder.

Now let's get into how the mechanics work — and this is where it starts getting interesting.

So remember at the beginning — there were Julie and Joe, the two guys who never existed, but they have nice pictures. And each of them held half a million shares. They founded the company with one million shares. Half for me, half for you. Each of them holds five hundred thousand shares. Does the number matter? Whether it's five hundred thousand or five million or fifty? Doesn't matter. Usually when we're involved in a company, I try to make sure the company has at least ten million shares.

Because at some point you also build what's called an ESOP — Employee Stock Option Plan — where you want to give employees options. You'd be surprised — if the company has a hundred shares and you come and say, listen sweetie, you're doing a great job, I want to give you a quarter of a share — you'd say, are you making fun of me? Are you out of your mind? But if I have ten million shares and I come to you, I say — listen, I'm giving you ten thousand shares. You say — wow, sounds good, sounds really good. How many shares does the company have? Doesn't matter. Great, thanks a lot. That's it.

That's why I always say — hold at least ten million shares.

You can always increase the shares. You just do a split, that's all. You say — every share is now ten shares. Super easy to do. There's also a Reverse Split. I've had cases where the number of shares kept shrinking for various reasons. We had to do a Reverse Split because after a while it started being like the Turkish lira.

Now let's remember what's happening here. This is the first deal. So the company is worth four million dollars — that was the Pre Money, right? Each share is worth four dollars. Now Mike the Angel Investor wants to invest one million dollars. So what happens? The company creates two hundred fifty thousand shares and sells them to Mike. Mike buys the shares from the company. Meaning — the money goes into the company. Since he bought two hundred fifty thousand shares at four dollars per share — that comes out to one million dollars. Post Money Valuation — that's the Pre plus the amount that came in — five million.

And here's what the company's Cap Table looks like. Joe has five hundred thousand shares, now he holds forty percent. Before he held fifty percent. Why? We increased the number of shares. Now you understand how dilution works — they don't dilute you. There's no dilution action, but raising money creates dilution as a Side Effect, because now you have to share the pie with more people.

Raising money is done by issuing new shares and selling them to investors, and that's why you get this thing.

We've reached Round A. With High Flying Ventures. Deal Structure — five million dollars at ten million Pre Money. Now since the company has one million two hundred fifty thousand shares — you divide ten by one million two hundred fifty thousand — and on my calculator that came out to eight dollars per share. Before it was four, now it's eight. There's internal logic here.

What does High Flying do? They want to invest five million. They issue six hundred twenty-five thousand shares and he buys them. Buying six hundred twenty-five thousand shares times eight dollars — comes out to five million dollars. Post Money is now fifteen, which is ten Pre Money plus five investment.

Joe will be diluted. The new investor holds a third of the company now — five out of fifteen. And the Angel Investor dropped from twenty to thirteen.

Round B. Fifteen million dollars at fifteen million dollars Pre Money. Pre Money was the previous Post Money. Nothing changed here, so the share price stays at eight.

It's much more convenient to work with the share price than to calculate dilutions and so on. Because if you work by share price — everything flows immediately in the most correct way. Work with share count. That's the most correct way, the simplest, and the clearest in the end. I'm raising money — it's not about dilutions. How many shares did I need to sell — and then everything follows from the fact that the pie changes.

Julie was fired, you remember? She still holds the shares. Just because you fired someone from the company doesn't mean you can take their shares.

Everyone will be diluted by fifty percent because these guys took fifty percent. These three took fifty percent of the company.

There's no such thing as intentional dilution. You issue more shares, someone bought them. That's what happens. By the way, even when you issue shares for the ESOP you dilute everyone. You simply added more shares. That's all that happened.

Julie is a Co-Founder. What happens when two founders don't get along? It's roughly like a divorce. Same thing. There's no standard arrangement. Some fight, some battle it out. That's why I always say — if you're going with a Co-Founder, make sure you have a really ugly agreement that spells out exactly who can fire whom, what happens in a termination, how things work, what the grounds for termination are. Otherwise it's madness.

In many cases there's vesting of four years for the founders as well.

Now we get to the last round — Ray Of Hope comes in and saves the world. He has his own Deal Structure — ten million dollars at a Pre Money of ten million, in a Down Turn. He puts in Participating Preferred Shares with Liquidation. The company has three point seven five million shares, so the share price — you divide one by the other — ten million — you get two dollars sixty-six.

The share price dropped from eight to two dollars sixty-six. And that's exactly what reflects the Down Round. The share price went down.

And then Ray Of Hope wants to invest ten million. So he buys that same number of shares. Look — in total we raised thirty-one million dollars. Over the life of the company we raised thirty-one million dollars. And here's what the ownership looks like. Ray Of Hope is sitting on fifty percent of the company now. When he came in, he brought the Pre Money Valuation down from thirty to ten, put in ten, took half the company.

Really, how can you do that? Because he's the investor. Because he says — I'm willing to pay two sixty-six. You want to sell me shares? Fine. You don't want to? There are ten other companies that need Ray Of Hope just as much as you do. You want my money? These are the terms. You don't want the terms? Go find another investor.

By the way, there are investors who specialize in distressed companies. Since the company was in trouble, that's what he did.

Now what happens next? The company raised thirty-one and was sold for forty million. So what's the waterfall?

Now we get to the most interesting part of any deal — how the money starts flowing downward.

So let's see. First of all, Ray of Hope invested ten million in Participating Preferred Shares. He gets his money back first because that's part of the terms. So he pulls out ten million dollars, and he's also first in liquidation rights.

So he pulls out twenty million dollars first because he was last in line. He was the one who saved the company. He's the ray of hope. Those were his terms.

And now we have twenty million dollars that need to be split among people who invested twenty-one million dollars. And they were nice to each other — everyone was still in the euphoria that this was a company that was going to do well, and none of them demanded liquidation rights ahead of the others. Meaning — everyone's sitting in the same spot. That happens sometimes too. So now everyone wants to split twenty million dollars among people who invested twenty-one million dollars.

He actually doesn't split with everyone at all. He ends up with more money. It's called the highest of. He takes the higher of the two. If he had to split with everyone, he would have gotten ninety-five cents on the dollar. He doesn't want that, he wants all his money back. So he exercises his participating right, exercises his liquidation right, and pulls out the money.

So Joe, after all his hard work, gets — zero. He ends up with zero. Why? Because the investors pull out first. The investors — more or less — got out by the skin of their teeth. I put in a million, I got back nine hundred fifty thousand. Not the end of the world. Somehow they saved me.

They knew the whole story we showed here. Everything we showed here was clear to them. But their alternative was to get zero, or to bring in someone with money who could maybe improve the situation and bring them to a point where the loss isn't terrible. Meaning, they went in here with a practical judgment and that's why they were willing to accept the Down Round, the Down Turn, all these terms — because that's exactly what happened.

Who got screwed? The entrepreneur. I showed you back then what I was left with from Rosh Intelligence System — a stock certificate for three shares. That's exactly the reason why. And I'm not alone. This happens endlessly. So you always have to be careful when someone says — he's the entrepreneur, he founded the company, it was sold for a hundred million dollars, he must have come out a millionaire. Sometimes not.

What was Joe's interest in even staying at the company? He could have said — dude, I'm not going to make a dime out of this.

A — people who build companies — it's their baby. Unlike investors for whom it's not their baby, they just want to make money. Entrepreneurs — this is their thing. They're identified with the company.

And between us — let's think for a moment that after it came out in the papers, in Globes, in Calcalist — Survivah was sold for forty million dollars and thirty-one million dollars was invested in the company. He walks around — hey guys, I was the entrepreneur, I founded the company. Look what a success. And it is a success — even though he didn't get a penny in the end. Nobody knows how much you made.

Really, nobody sees the waterfall. Remember that — the waterfall — you see how complicated it is.

I think many times, at the moment of truth when the deal is on the table, because of all the veto rights — a negotiation basically opens up between all the parties involved, because the sting of a deal that's borderline like this and nobody wants to lose.

In deals that I did — there were discussions but there were no wars. In the end the interpretation was pretty unambiguous. At the beginning there was confusion, but in the end the interpretations were generally unambiguous.

Nobody got anything, only the investors somehow got out by the skin of their teeth. But it happens.

Sometimes the investors want the employees to get something anyway because it gives them a bad reputation. They gave to the employees.

I even did that myself. In one of the companies I sold, in my opinion the employees didn't have enough money. So I convinced everyone to take — I don't remember how many millions of dollars anymore — and put them as a bonus for the employees. It happens when you look at it and say — in the end, the ones who built the company weren't me, it was all the people who worked with me. There's no money left for the employees. Not fair.

Many times this also happens through the buyer. Sometimes the buyer looks at the company and says — listen, you screwed over the employees, they're going to leave. And then the buyer adds a bonus. He says — I'm giving you thirty-five million and another five million will be a bonus for the employees.

This is one of the best-kept secrets. This is the waterfall.

Since we're pretty close to the end, I want to talk about something completely different. We gave you super interesting homework and I want to talk about it. We'll bring it up for discussion in the next meeting. Why? Because when I started making this presentation and working on it, it turned out I was about seventy percent through the presentation. There's another thirty percent we won't get to today.

Next week, the next meeting is our last meeting. This article, in my eyes, was a real bonanza. To say all the things that I've said throughout the entire course — in one article, by someone else, not by me. So that was really fantastic. And I really want to do this as a summary of the course — the last review of the course, not from the horse's mouth, but from that other horse's mouth. Meaning, to quote them and discuss what they're doing that we've been recommending all along, and what they're doing that I don't recommend. But it doesn't matter, they managed to raise something like two hundred million dollars. I told you — raise as much as you can. So that they did.

Your homework is saved with us, we'll go through it. But I really want to do it in the next meeting, to go through all these details, because it'll give us a fantastic opportunity to review most of the principles of what we've been talking about here — they appear in the article. It just blew me away. Seeing them talk about exactly all the things we've been talking about — gave me positive reinforcement that I'm not the only crazy one and that they're worth two billion dollars.

There's still time for questions, I don't mind. The continuation is — How to build a smart-up, not a start-up. That's what we would tell Joe to do this time. Just one small thing — Don't do that.

Next time, if we have time, we'll go through this continuation.

Oh! Okay, I'll say a couple of words about SAFE. What is SAFE? Remember that the share price or company valuation — it's how much people are willing to pay. What happened is that angel investors feel they're unable to set a price for the company since they don't sit in the market, they're not professional investors. They're just putting in two hundred fifty thousand dollars, fifty thousand dollars, twenty-five thousand dollars. They don't know what the company is worth. So they defer that question to the first round that will be led by professional investors — Round A usually. Meaning, they simply say — since I don't know the price, I trust that the next price will determine it and I get a bonus. Usually they get some sort of twenty percent discount. They set some maximum price that says — I want to get this at no more than this price in any case. They often put in some protections for themselves for any trouble that might come. But that's more or less, in plain English — let's defer the discussion about the price, let someone else decide. That's what SAFE means in a nutshell.

Exactly. They say — I don't understand any of this, a savior will come and solve the problem. They don't know. They say — I can't determine this, let a professional investor come and decide. Not that the professional investor has some magic formula, but at least he's putting in five million dollars, so it's likely he'll think about it more than I do when I'm putting in fifty thousand dollars.

Guys, it was fun. Thanks, it was excellent. Thank you very much, it was very interesting. Something that really broadened my horizons.

This lecture explores one of the most critical reasons startups fail: they run out of money. While the statement may sound obvious, the session delves deeply into the financial mechanics behind startup funding, venture capital dynamics, and the often-misunderstood economics of building a company. The course, called SmartUp, is described as a methodology for building successful companies and a school for CEOs — recognizing that the founder-CEO role is complex, experience-dependent, and inherently lonely. The program's goal is not to guarantee success but to improve the odds statistically, ideally moving the success rate from one in ten to one in three.

Success is defined by three criteria that must work in harmony: the company is profitable, growing fast, and operating with limited capital. Achieving all three simultaneously is compared to a concert where every instrument must play together — otherwise the result is noise. Importantly, success can be reached well before a major exit or billionaire status.

The lecture follows a fictional entrepreneur named Joe, an engineer with an idea for an online psychology platform, through the full startup funding lifecycle. Starting with personal savings and money from family and friends, Joe progresses through angel investment, multiple VC rounds, and eventually a significant funding journey. Along the way, the audience learns how company valuations are set — not by objective formulas but by market perception and what investors are willing to pay. A real-world case study involving ZoomInfo illustrates how dramatically market sentiment can shift valuations, with the company swinging from a peak of twenty-six billion dollars down to under one billion despite strong revenue and profitability.

A particularly revealing segment covers the "waterfall" — the order in which investors, founders, and employees receive proceeds when a company is sold. The lecture demonstrates that even in a successful acquisition, founders and employees can walk away with little or nothing due to investor protections and liquidation preferences. This is described as one of the best-kept secrets in the startup world. The session also introduces the concept of a SAFE note, explaining how early angel investors defer company valuation to later professional investors, typically receiving a discount as compensation for their early risk.

The lecture closes by previewing the next and final session, which will contrast the conventional startup approach with the SmartUp methodology — essentially advising founders on how to navigate the funding minefield more wisely and build companies that are sustainable rather than simply venture-backed.
